chapter: First jobs and New Orleans players
title: Favorite trumpeters and the Celestin versus Sam Morgan contest
summary: He ranks Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and others, and tells of the 1925 contest where Celestin's wah-wah mute beat Morgan.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Who were your favorite trumpet players? Who did you like to play with? Who were the best ones in the city and all that you heard those days?

Well, I'll tell you, we had quite a few good trumpet players. I'd say Sam Morgan, Buddy P. King, and we had Punch. He was a nice trumpet player at that time. Rain A was one of the next greatest to Sam Morgan, I think, with Tornation. But Sam had a sweet Tornation at the time. And Rain A, he come with the best second tone of the city that we know. We had several good ones. And probably all of them was good back in them days. But they had different favorites and so forth like that. Well, Buddy T. P., we would say at that time, well, he was known as Bell House. And we said, it was a lot of ragtime. They called it Bell House. It was a ragtime. So, well, that's what he would come with a bucket in his hand. And he would blow in the bucket. And he'd get to the hall, they'd tell Buddy, Boy, blow in the bucket, Buddy. So they wanted to hear Buddy blow in the bucket. So at that time, we didn't hear about no mutes or nothing like that. Or no hats or the derby like the orchestra used, you know. Then later years, well, Sam had held the city for, as I know, for Sam Morgan to round by 25. Then we had what you call a contest at Pelican in 1925. Well, at that time, it was Celestan and Sam Morgan. They had a contest. Well, quite naturally, the people had never heard a wah-wah mute. So Celestan put that wah-wah mute in his trumpet. And he began to come on there with my Josephine, which it was a steal from some of these days.
Yeah, the tune and something like that.

And the people never had heard it. And he put that mute in there and making that wah-wah. Well, they give him the cup. So that from then on, Celestan held the whole city. And it wasn't soon later that Sam went on because he took a stroke, you know. Yeah. But Sam had held the city for many years. Went all on the coast and everywhere with Sam Morgan. And they would meet up out there like on a Sunday. Or they would meet up on the corner and they would get in the bucket. And they would hook them tailgates together. And one truck couldn't pull off without the oven. And sometimes the people would be cooking and they would forget that they were cooking. And sometimes the pots would burn up. People would forget about their cooking and so much music going on in the corner. People would forget their cooking and come to the window. And sometimes they would stay in the window and something could leave out of the house. Sometimes they would battle all that for about an hour. Sometimes maybe a little long. But I tell you, everybody, it seemed like it wasn't a Sunday that you didn't hear some kind of a band of music. You'd hear something every Sunday. Bands of music, dance hall was all over the city. Everywhere people was going for dances. And it looked like everybody was taken to dances. And it looked like everybody had rhythm in their feet. So if you could play music, don't care what it was, that you would welcome in any of the homes, if you know anything, any kind of instrument, guitar, a piano, well them were the most things that they was using in the homes at those particular times. People, they would like you to play guitar. Even on the guitar player would come in at night. Say sometime it would be 2 o'clock, 3 o'clock in the morning. Sometime like my father, he would come home 3 o'clock in the morning. He would get the blues, he would sit on the back step in the yard all night long with the guitar. And play that guitar and it looked like the lady got the sweeter that music sounded. And people would want to hear it.
